title: What Schools Should Do With the Billions Coming Their Way
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that districts receiving roughly $190 billion in federal pandemic relief should invest in something usually overlooked: a knowledge-building elementary curriculum. She first urges caution about the label evidence-based, since a single study, short-term trials or weak control groups can all qualify. She notes that most tutoring targets supposed comprehension skills and so mirrors the failing classroom approach, when background knowledge and vocabulary drive comprehension. She then lists practical steps: adopt a coherent curriculum across grades, name examples such as Core Knowledge Language Arts and Wit & Wisdom, support teachers with curriculum-specific training, resist retreating to skills for political reasons, and supplement rather than build from scratch. The piece frames the money as a one-time chance to address decades of learning loss for the most vulnerable students.
points: Wexler recommends spending relief funds on a knowledge-building elementary curriculum rather than one-time purchases.
She warns that evidence-based can mean a single favorable study, short trials, or a weak comparison group.
Much tutoring drills comprehension skills on random easy texts and inherits the weakness of the standard curriculum.
Consistent curriculum across grades matters because knowledge builds gradually and cumulatively.
Districts should adopt an existing curriculum and supplement it, since most educators are not trained to write curriculum from scratch.
quotes: That sounds straightforward, but the term could just mean there’s one study showing positive effects. Meanwhile, there could be—and often are—more studies that go the other way.

That approach mirrors the standard elementary curriculum, and it won’t work any better with tutoring than it has in the classroom. Reading comprehension depends far more on academic knowledge and vocabulary than on abstract “skill”—which is probably why studies show that with reading tutoring, there’s “a pattern of declining returns” at higher grade levels.

Because of the dominance of reading and math at lower grade levels, kids often arrive at high school without the background knowledge they need to succeed. That’s particularly true if they’ve had limited opportunities to acquire academic knowledge outside school.
It’s best to use the same curriculum across as many grades as possible. Building knowledge is a gradual, cumulative process.

But withholding academic knowledge from children and then holding them accountable for knowing it, as we currently do, is the essence of unfairness. And large majorities of students lack basic knowledge of history and civics, something that jeopardizes not only their own futures but the future of our democracy.

But rather than trying to reinvent the wheel, districts should adopt an existing curriculum and add or substitute materials that cover what they feel is missing. Creating curriculum from scratch is hard, and most educators haven’t been trained to do it.
